prompt: Some people believe that growing up in a big city is the best preparation for life, because a young person meets many kinds of people and has more opportunities close at hand. Others believe a smaller town or the countryside is better, because life is calmer and people know and look out for one another. Which do you think is the better place to grow up? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response names what growing up should give a young person and judges each place against it, rather than listing what each has. Credit specific scenes, a crowded subway ride or a neighbour who notices when something is wrong, over general claims. A writer who admits one real advantage of the other side and explains why it matters less should be rewarded.
accessibility_note: Students who have lived in only one kind of place can argue from that experience or from visits, relatives, books and films; no travel is required.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "I had exactly ten minutes before my mother got home, and the kitchen still looked like a storm had passed through it."
guidance: A strong story uses the time limit to build tension and makes the reader care why the mess happened and what the narrator is trying to hide or fix. Reward a plan that goes wrong in a believable way and an ending that changes something between the narrator and the mother, not only whether the kitchen got clean.
accessibility_note: Any parent, guardian or older relative works in the story, and the mess can come from anything a student can imagine, cooking, a project or a pet.

prompt: Some people say it is better to spend money on experiences, such as trips, concerts or classes, because memories last longer than objects. Others say it is better to spend on things that last, such as a good bicycle, books or tools, because they can be used again and again. Which do you think is the wiser way to spend money? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response explains what makes spending worthwhile, lasting enjoyment, usefulness or what it teaches, and applies that standard to both sides. Small, concrete examples, a museum visit or a well-used pair of shoes, are as good as large ones. Credit a writer who tests their view against a case where it seems not to hold.
accessibility_note: The examples can be small and free or nearly free, such as a library visit or a borrowed tool, so the prompt does not reward students whose families spend more.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The new student sat down in my seat on the first day, and I decided not to say anything."
guidance: A strong story makes the narrator's choice to stay quiet matter and shows its consequences over time, whether the two become friends, rivals or something in between. Reward realistic dialogue and an ending that reveals something about the narrator's character.
accessibility_note: The setting can be any class, club, team or activity with assigned or usual seats, so no particular school experience is assumed.

prompt: Some families pay children for doing chores, believing it teaches them that work earns money and helps them learn to manage it. Other families believe chores should be done without pay, because everyone who lives in a home shares the work of keeping it running. Which approach do you think is better? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response considers what each approach teaches beyond the chores themselves, about money, responsibility or belonging. Credit specific examples, a family rule, a friend's arrangement or a story, over general statements. The best essays address what happens when a child refuses a paid chore, or does an unpaid one badly.
accessibility_note: Students can argue from their own family, from friends' families or from books and shows, and either position can be argued well whatever arrangement the writer has at home.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "My grandmother handed me her worn recipe card and told me that this time I would make it myself."
guidance: A strong story uses the cooking as a way into the relationship: what the recipe means to the grandmother and what the narrator learns while making it. Reward sensory detail and a moment of difficulty or mistake. The ending should show what was passed on, not only whether the food turned out well.
accessibility_note: Any older relative or family friend can be the character, and the dish can be anything from any tradition, so no particular background is assumed.

prompt: Some people believe that in school and in work it matters most to be quick, because the world moves fast and opportunities go to those who act first. Others believe it matters more to be careful, because a fast mistake can cost more than a slow success. Which quality do you think is more important for a student your age, speed or care? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response defines both qualities and shows where each helps or hurts, using a timed test, a project, a sport or a job. Credit a writer who explains when their choice should give way to the other. Specific moments of rushing or of taking too long carry more weight than general advice.
accessibility_note: Every student has rushed something or taken too long on something, so the prompt needs no special experience, and examples from games, hobbies or home are as valid as school ones.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The score was tied, the whistle was about to blow, and the coach was looking straight at me."
guidance: A strong story builds the pressure of the moment and makes the reader understand what is at stake for the narrator beyond winning. Reward a character who makes a choice, and an ending that shows how the moment changed the narrator, whatever the result.
accessibility_note: The competition can be any team or individual activity, a sport, a debate, a quiz or a game, so students who do not play sports can still write the story.

prompt: Some people believe young people should follow the news every day so that they understand the world they will soon help to run. Others believe that following the news too closely makes people anxious and gives them little they can act on. How closely do you think a person your age should follow the news? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response takes a clear position on how much news is useful and explains why, rather than saying news is simply good or bad. Credit a writer who distinguishes between kinds of news or ways of following it. Specific examples of a story that helped or worried the writer should support the argument.
accessibility_note: The prompt does not require access to newspapers or devices; students can argue from conversations at home, at school or in their community, and either position can be argued well.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "Halfway up the trail, my friend sat down on a rock and said she was not going any farther."
guidance: A strong story turns on the friendship: why the friend stopped and what the narrator decides to do about it. Reward dialogue that reveals both characters and a decision that costs the narrator something. The ending should resolve the conflict between them, not only the hike.
accessibility_note: The walk can be on any path, a park, a hill or a city route, so no particular outdoor experience is needed.

prompt: Some people believe that famous athletes, musicians and actors have a duty to set a good example, because many young people copy what they do. Others believe famous people should be judged only on their work, and that their private choices are their own business. Which view do you agree with? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience, your reading, or your observation.
guidance: A strong response explains where responsibility comes from, influence, choice or fame itself, and applies that reasoning to a specific case. Credit a writer who considers whether young people should copy celebrities at all. Avoid rewarding long summaries of a celebrity's life; the argument should do the work.
accessibility_note: Students can draw on any well-known person from sports, music, games, books or their own community, so no particular interest in celebrities is assumed.

prompt: Write a story that begins with the following sentence: "The sign on the shop door said 'Help Wanted,' and before I could change my mind, I walked in."
guidance: A strong story makes the reader understand why the narrator wanted the job and what they risked by walking in. Reward a believable interview or first day, with a character on the other side of the counter who feels real. The ending should show what the narrator gained or learned, whether or not they got the job.
accessibility_note: The shop can be any business a student can imagine, and the story needs no real work experience, only a person deciding to ask for a chance.
